To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
adaptive broadcasting can be solved efficiently in networks with a constant number of faulty nodes.
adaptive broadcasting in networks with faulty nodes can be solved efficiently.

(1) adaptive broadcasting is possible in time O(log2n); (2) the algorithm is optimal, in the sense that no adaptive broadcasting algorithm can work faster than O(log2 n); and (3) the algorithm is robust, in the sense of being resilient to the presence of a large number of faulty nodes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (i) What is the worst-case running time of adaptive broadcasting in a completely connected network? (ii) Can the running time be reduced by allowing non-adaptive scheduling? (iii) How does broadcasting time depend on the number of faulty nodes?

the following question: What is the time complexity of broadcasting in a network of n nodes with k faulty nodes, if the number of faulty nodes is a small constant fraction of n and the broadcasting algorithm is allowed to adapt to the current state of the network.

the following questions. What is the worst-case time of broadcasting in the presence of faults? How many faulty nodes can be tolerated? Can the broadcasting time be made independent of the network size n?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there exists an adaptive broadcasting algorithm that works in time O(log2n) and is optimal in the worst-case.
the problem of adaptive broadcasting is solved for all networks with bounded number of faults.
the problem of adaptive broadcasting in the presence of faulty nodes is in the complexity class NC1.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the time needed for broadcasting is logarithmic in the number of nodes.
we have developed a new technique for adaptive broadcasting, which we call the “broadcasting with the help of the faulty nodes” approach.
the time required for broadcasting in a network with k faulty nodes is bounded above by O(log n), and below by Omega(k log n).
The main takeaway from our work is that
, under a certain model of fault tolerance, broadcasting in a completely connected network can be done in time logarithmic in the number of nodes.
adaptive broadcasting in the presence of faulty nodes is possible with a small number of faulty nodes.
the number of faults does not have to be known in advance.
